sections.title: Physical & Logical Topologies
sections.content:
A topology is how a network is arranged (physical = the wiring; logical = how data actually flows).
Star — every node connects to a central switch. The dominant LAN topology: easy to troubleshoot, one failed link affects only one host, but the central device is a single point of failure.
Mesh — nodes interconnect with many paths. Full mesh = every node to every other (maximum redundancy, expensive); partial mesh balances cost and redundancy. Common in WANs.
Bus — all nodes share one backbone cable (legacy; one break kills the segment).
Ring — each node connects to two neighbors in a loop (legacy; token-based).
Hybrid — a mix, e.g., a star-of-stars (star-bus). Most real networks are hybrids.
Point-to-point — a direct link between exactly two nodes (a WAN leased line).
Hub-and-spoke — a central hub site with branch spokes (common WAN design).
exam_tips: Star is the standard LAN topology; its weakness is the central switch as a single point of failure.
Full mesh gives maximum redundancy but cost grows fast: n(n-1)/2 links.

sections.title: Network Architectures
sections.content:
Three-tier hierarchical model (campus):
Core — high-speed backbone that moves traffic fast; no packet manipulation.
Distribution (aggregation) — policy, routing between VLANs, ACLs, redundancy.
Access (edge) — where end devices plug in; switch ports, PoE, VLAN assignment.
Collapsed core — combines core and distribution into one layer for smaller networks.
Spine-and-leaf — the modern data center design: every leaf (access) switch connects to every spine switch. Predictable low latency, easy to scale horizontally, ideal for east-west (server-to-server) traffic.
Traffic flows: north-south = client-to-server (in/out of the data center); east-west = server-to-server (within it). Virtualization and microservices made east-west traffic dominant, which spine-leaf handles well.
exam_tips: Three-tier = Core / Distribution / Access. Collapsed core merges core + distribution for smaller sites.
Spine-and-leaf is built for east-west (server-to-server) data-center traffic.

sections.title: Network Types & Scope
sections.content:
By geographic scope:
PAN — Personal Area Network (Bluetooth, a few meters).
LAN — Local Area Network (a building/campus).
WLAN — Wireless LAN (Wi-Fi).
CAN — Campus Area Network (a group of nearby buildings).
MAN — Metropolitan Area Network (a city).
WAN — Wide Area Network (across cities/countries; the internet is the biggest WAN).
Specialized: SAN (Storage Area Network — block storage fabric), SDWAN, and the difference between a WAN (you connect sites over provider links) and a LAN (you own the local gear).
Client-server vs peer-to-peer: client-server centralizes resources/management on servers; peer-to-peer shares resources directly between hosts with no central server (simpler, harder to secure/manage at scale).
exam_tips: Scope order small to large: PAN -> LAN -> CAN -> MAN -> WAN.
Don't confuse SAN (storage fabric) with WAN (wide-area). They sound alike but are unrelated.

concept_cards.hook: Every node connects to a central switch. The standard LAN layout — easy to manage, but the central device is a single point of failure.
A topology where every node links directly to every other node, giving maximum redundancy at high cost: n(n-1)/2 links.
A hierarchical campus design of Core (fast backbone), Distribution (routing/policy), and Access (end-device ports).
A data-center architecture where every leaf switch connects to every spine switch, giving predictable low latency for east-west traffic and easy horizontal scaling.
North-south is client-to-server traffic in/out of the data center; east-west is server-to-server traffic within it.
A design that merges the core and distribution layers into one, used in smaller networks that don't need a separate backbone layer.
A WAN topology with a central hub site to which all branch (spoke) sites connect, simplifying management but making the hub critical.
Client-server centralizes resources and control on dedicated servers; peer-to-peer shares resources directly between equal hosts with no central server.

practice_questions.q: Which topology connects every node to a central switch and is standard for LANs?
practice_questions.explanation: The star topology centers on a switch and is the dominant wired-LAN layout.

practice_questions.q: How many links does a full mesh of 5 nodes require?
Traffic flowing between servers inside a data center is described as:
practice_questions.explanation: East-west is server-to-server traffic within the data center; north-south is client-to-server.

practice_questions.q: Which modern data-center design connects every access switch to every spine switch?
practice_questions.explanation: Spine-and-leaf gives predictable low latency and scales horizontally for east-west traffic.

practice_questions.q: In the three-tier model, which layer provides the high-speed backbone with no packet manipulation?
practice_questions.explanation: The core layer moves traffic as fast as possible; policy/routing happens at distribution.

practice_questions.q: Which network type spans a single metropolitan area?
practice_questions.explanation: A Metropolitan Area Network covers a city-sized area, larger than a campus (CAN), smaller than a WAN.

practice_questions.q: A Bluetooth connection between a phone and headset forms which type of network?
practice_questions.explanation: A Personal Area Network spans a few meters around a person's devices.

practice_questions.q: Which design merges the core and distribution layers for smaller networks?
practice_questions.explanation: A collapsed core combines core and distribution where a separate backbone isn't needed.

practice_questions.q: In which architecture do hosts share resources directly with no central server?
practice_questions.explanation: Peer-to-peer shares resources between equal hosts; client-server centralizes on servers.

practice_questions.q: Which WAN topology has branch 'spoke' sites all connecting to one central site?
practice_questions.explanation: Hub-and-spoke centralizes connectivity through a hub site; simple but the hub is critical.
